741: The present chapter reports and interprets the findings of the three experiments. Experiment I addresses the influence of production location and storage period on the grain quality of three aromatic landraces; Experiment II the quality of seven processed and cooked products prepared from ten cultivars; and Experiment III the sensory and nutritional quality of plain and vegetable-fortified idli. All tables and figures in this chapter are numbered consecutively in the series 4.1 onwards.
744: This experiment quantified the extent to which production location, landrace and duration of post-harvest storage govern the grain quality of three traditional aromatic rices of West Bengal. The landraces examined were Gobindabhog (V1), Radhunipagal (V2) and Kalojira (V3), procured respectively from Nadia (L1), Purba Bardhaman (L2) and Birbhum/Howrah (L3). Each lot was evaluated as fresh paddy (S1) and again at 4 months (S2), 8 months (S3) and 12 months (S4) after harvest. All lots were held at Bidhan Chandra Krishi Viswavidyalaya, Mohanpur, under identical ambient conditions, so that the location factor denotes the site of production alone. The experiment followed a factorial randomised block design with three replications and was repeated in 2022–23 and 2023–24. Thirty-eight parameters were recorded and are presented under seven heads: physical, sensory, nutritional, anti-nutritional, colour, mineral and amino acid attributes. Data were subjected to analysis of variance appropriate to a three-factor factorial randomised block design (Das and Giri, 1986), with year incorporated as an additional factor. The year × treatment interactions proved non-significant for the majority of parameters; all means reported below are therefore pooled over the two years. SEm, CD at the 5% level and CV were computed from the pooled error mean square with 140 degrees of freedom. Means sharing a common letter do not differ significantly at the 5% level by the least significant difference test. In the tables, GB, RP and KJ denote the three landraces in the order given above. Amino acids were assayed on freshly harvested grain alone; Section 4.7 consequently reports S1 means only and records no effect of storage.
749: Location exerted a highly significant effect on hulling. The highest value, 77.02%, was recorded at Nadia, followed by Purba Bardhaman with 75.59% and Birbhum/Howrah with 75.28%. No two locations shared a letter group, each therefore differing significantly from the remaining two, and the extremes were separated by 1.73 percentage points.
751: Varietal differences were equally distinct, attaining significance at the 1% level. Kalojira recorded the highest value, 77.52%, followed by Gobindabhog with 75.78% and Radhunipagal with 74.58%. All three landraces were statistically discrete, Kalojira exceeding Radhunipagal by 2.94 percentage points.
753: Storage period altered hulling significantly at the 1% level. In order of sampling, the values were 76.82% in fresh paddy, 76.92% at 4 months, 74.30% at 8 months and 75.81% at 12 months, the maximum thus occurring at 4 months and the minimum at 8 months. Across the twelve-month period the value declined by 1.3%.
755: The location × variety interaction was highly significant. Kalojira at Nadia constituted the superior combination with 78.55%, and Radhunipagal at Birbhum/Howrah the inferior one with 73.99%. The varietal sequence Kalojira, Gobindabhog, Radhunipagal was maintained at every location; the interaction consequently modified the magnitude of the varietal differences rather than their direction.
756: The location × storage interaction was significant at the 1% level. The highest mean, 78.89%, was recorded for Nadia at 4 months and the lowest, 73.81%, for Purba Bardhaman at 8 months. Between fresh paddy and 12 months the value shifted by -1.3% at Nadia, -1.2% at Purba Bardhaman and -1.4% at Birbhum/Howrah. The magnitude of change was comparable across locations, storage having been conducted at a single site and having acted uniformly on grain of every provenance.
757: The variety × storage interaction was significant at the 1% level. The highest mean, 79.01%, was recorded for Kalojira in fresh paddy and the lowest, 73.45%, for Radhunipagal at 8 months. Over twelve months Gobindabhog changed by -0.7%, Radhunipagal by -1.3% and Kalojira by -2.0%. The three landraces shifted by nearly equivalent margins, storage having affected them comparably.
758: The three-way interaction was highly significant. Among the thirty six treatment combinations, the maximum value of 80.20% was recorded by Kalojira grown at Nadia and sampled at 4 months, and the minimum of 72.38% by Gobindabhog grown at Birbhum/Howrah and sampled at 8 months, a spread of 7.82 percentage points. This range appreciably exceeded that generated by any single factor in isolation, the three factors having operated jointly; a favourable outcome therefore required all three to be specified concurrently.
767: Hulling expresses the proportion of brown rice recovered upon removal of the husk. The divergence among the three locations indicates that the site of production materially conditions this trait. Li et al. (2018) demonstrated that temperature, insolation and humidity during the weeks following flowering influence milling outturn more strongly than most other quality attributes. Singh et al. (2000) and Mahendra et al. (2019) reported comparable differentiation among small- and medium-grained Indian aromatic rices, while Patra et al. (2024) recorded hulling of 77.6 to 77.9% in the West Bengal aromatic landrace Tulaipanji, a range closely corroborating the value obtained here for Kalojira. Wongpornchai et al. (2004) and Zhou et al. (2002) likewise attributed milling behaviour to the moisture status of the grain rather than to any durable chemical alteration, and Müller et al. (2022), reviewing a broad body of post-harvest work, concluded that maintenance of hygroscopic equilibrium in stored grain constitutes the single most decisive factor in preserving milling quality.
771: Location exerted a highly significant effect on milling. The highest value, 71.38%, was recorded at Birbhum/Howrah, followed by Nadia with 70.30% and Purba Bardhaman with 68.99%. The three locations resolved into discrete letter groups, each differing significantly from the others, with a margin of 2.39 percentage points separating the superior from the inferior site.
773: Varietal differences were equally distinct, attaining significance at the 1% level. Kalojira recorded the highest value, 71.63%, followed by Gobindabhog with 70.87% and Radhunipagal with 68.17%. All three landraces were statistically discrete, Kalojira exceeding Radhunipagal by 3.47 percentage points.
775: Storage period altered milling to a highly significant degree. In order of sampling, the values were 70.21% in fresh paddy, 71.49% at 4 months, 68.62% at 8 months and 70.56% at 12 months, the maximum occurring at 4 months and the minimum at 8 months. Over the full year the value increased by 0.5%.
777: The location × variety interaction was significant at the 1% level. Kalojira at Birbhum/Howrah constituted the superior combination with 72.89%, and Radhunipagal at Purba Bardhaman the inferior one with 66.90%. The varietal order Kalojira, Gobindabhog, Radhunipagal remained invariant across locations; the interaction therefore altered the magnitude of the varietal margin but not its sign.
778: The location × storage interaction was non-significant. The highest mean, 72.69%, was recorded for Birbhum/Howrah at 4 months and the lowest, 67.55%, for Purba Bardhaman at 8 months. Between fresh paddy and 12 months of storage the change amounted to +0.6% at Nadia, +0.8% at Purba Bardhaman and +0.2% at Birbhum/Howrah. All three locations shifted by closely comparable margins, the effect of storage proving independent of the district of origin.
779: The variety × storage interaction was likewise non-significant. The highest mean, 72.94%, was recorded for Kalojira at 4 months and the lowest, 66.42%, for Radhunipagal at 8 months. Over twelve months the change amounted to +0.2% in Gobindabhog, +0.3% in Radhunipagal and +1.0% in Kalojira. The three landraces changed by comparable margins and thus responded to storage in a uniform manner.
780: The three-factor interaction was non-significant. Among the thirty six treatment combinations, the maximum value of 73.88% was recorded by Kalojira grown at Birbhum/Howrah and sampled at 4 months, and the minimum of 65.21% by Radhunipagal grown at Purba Bardhaman and sampled at 8 months. Given the non-significance of this term, these extreme cells cannot be interpreted as genuine differences in isolation, and the main effects afford the more reliable inference.
789: Milling percentage denotes the weight of polished rice recovered from the original paddy and, as the figure determining the miller's return on a given lot, carries direct commercial significance. Milling recovery is contingent upon the compactness of endosperm packing, which is in turn established by the weather prevailing during grain filling. Tsado et al. (2015) established that cracking and breakage in milled rice depend strongly on cultivar and deteriorate as the duration of paddy storage extends. Müller et al. (2022) corroborated this conclusion and further observed that both cultivar and drying history govern the extent of breakage subsequently incurred during polishing. Chrastil and Zarins (1992) demonstrated this alteration in the protein of stored rice, and Zhou et al. (2015) placed it at the centre of their explanation of rice ageing.
793: Location exerted a highly significant effect on head rice recovery. The highest value, 64.38%, was recorded at Birbhum/Howrah, followed by Purba Bardhaman with 64.08% and Nadia with 62.87%. Each location occupied a discrete letter group, matching neither of the others, and the spread from the superior to the inferior site amounted to 1.52 percentage points.
795: The three landraces likewise differed among themselves, the varietal effect being highly significant. Kalojira recorded the highest value, 67.07%, followed by Radhunipagal with 62.26% and Gobindabhog with 62.00%. Each landrace occupied a discrete letter group, Kalojira exceeding Gobindabhog by 5.07 percentage points.
797: Storage period altered head rice recovery to a highly significant degree. In order of sampling, the values were 62.77% in fresh paddy, 64.06% at 4 months, 64.90% at 8 months and 63.37% at 12 months, the maximum occurring at 8 months and the minimum in fresh paddy. Over the full year the value increased by 1.0%.
799: The location × variety interaction was highly significant. Kalojira at Birbhum/Howrah constituted the superior combination with 68.88%, and Gobindabhog at Nadia the inferior one with 60.53%. The varietal order was not conserved across sites: at Nadia the sequence ran Kalojira, Radhunipagal, Gobindabhog; at Purba Bardhaman, Kalojira, Gobindabhog, Radhunipagal; and at Birbhum/Howrah, Kalojira, Radhunipagal, Gobindabhog. Rank reversal of this order establishes that the landraces responded differentially to the three environments.
800: The location × storage term fell short of significance. The highest mean, 65.64%, was recorded for Birbhum/Howrah at 8 months and the lowest, 62.12%, for Nadia in fresh paddy. Between fresh paddy and 12 months of storage the change amounted to +0.4% at Nadia, +1.4% at Purba Bardhaman and +1.1% at Birbhum/Howrah. The three locations shifted by nearly equivalent margins, the district of production exerting negligible influence on the action of storage.
801: The variety × storage term likewise fell short of significance. The highest mean, 68.22%, was recorded for Kalojira at 8 months and the lowest, 60.90%, for Gobindabhog in fresh paddy. Over twelve months the change amounted to +1.3% in Gobindabhog, +0.3% in Radhunipagal and +1.3% in Kalojira. The magnitude of change was comparable in all three landraces, storage having acted upon them equivalently.
802: The three-factor interaction was non-significant. Among the thirty six treatment combinations, the maximum value of 70.10% was recorded by Kalojira grown at Birbhum/Howrah and sampled at 8 months, and the minimum of 59.64% by Gobindabhog grown at Nadia and sampled at 12 months. Given the non-significance of this term, these extreme cells cannot be construed as genuine differences in isolation, and the main effects afford the more reliable inference.
811: Head rice recovery enumerates only the whole, unbroken grains. Since broken rice commands a substantially lower price than whole rice, this parameter frequently represents the most commercially consequential of the milling figures. Li et al. (2018) reported an equivalent balance, milling quality being governed more by the seed than by the field. The margin between landraces greatly exceeded that between locations, a pattern concordant with Li et al. (2018), who determined that milling quality is conditioned more by genotype than by growing environment. The underlying mechanism appears to be the same hardening described in respect of milling percentage, whereby the kernel acquires greater resistance to cracking (Zhou et al., 2002; Zhou et al., 2015). These findings suggest that the benefit conferred by ageing operates only up to a threshold. A miller may therefore apply a single ageing regime across all three landraces, while still selecting landrace and location in conjunction.
815: Location exerted a highly significant effect on the L/B ratio. The highest value, 1.865, was recorded at Birbhum/Howrah, followed by Nadia with 1.831 and Purba Bardhaman with 1.607. All three locations were statistically discrete, differing significantly among themselves, and the gap between the superior and inferior sites amounted to 0.258.
